## descendants de Koré
:::::: columns
::: {.column width="25%"}
:::

::: {.column width="5%"}
:::

::: {.column .smaller width="69%"}
Ils ne sont ni des gens d'armes, ni fonctionnaires, ni mercenaires 
mais des **portiers-gardiens** du temple et de ses trésors, des **chantres**, 
des hommes du Dieu de leur vie, guidés par la fidélité à leur Seigneur, habités du souvenir des oeuvres de l'Eternel, 
des hommes de coeur, émotionnels, des artistes maniant la harpe, la flûte, le chant et la poésie. 
:::
::::::
::: notes
ce sont des serviteurs épris de vérité et de justice, sensibles à la soif spirituelle, interrogés par les paradoxes, insultés par leurs contemporains irreligieux, mais concernés par le sort désastreux échu à leur peuple, 
un groupe solidaire d'hommes de prière relevant le défi de l'intercession pour une cause apparement perdue, soucieux de transmettre à la génération suivante la véritable connaissance de Dieu, et qui s'accrochent à conserver toujours l' espérance du salut parce qu'ils ont reconnu l'amour indéfectible de Dieu pour son peuple.
4. descendant de Koré 
du temps de Moise, de Samuel/David, de Josaphat, d Ezechias, de retour d exil a Babylone

1. Moïse (L'Exode) :  autour de 1250 av. J.-C. au temps du règne du pharaon Ramsès II.
​2. Le roi David : ~1010 à 970 av. J.-C.
​3. Le roi Josaphat : ~873 à 849 av. J.-C.
​4. Le roi Ézéchias : ~716 à 687 av. J.-C. célèbre pour ses réformes religieuses et pour avoir résiste au siège du roi assyrien Sennachérib en 701 av. J.-C.
​5. Le retour d'exil : ~538 av. J.-C. par l edit du roi Cyrus
:::

1. s'adresse au seul Dieu vivant
2. à des oreilles pour entendre 3. le témoignage des pères
4. et des yeux pour voir la main de Dieu dans l'histoire"

- calibrons notre compréhension avec les histoires de la Bible et créons les occasions de témoignage pour raconter ce que Dieu a fait pour nous.

- histoire que Dieu a écrite: Paque / Cene / Réforme, réveils;

## où sont les ennemis ?

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="35%"}

:::

::: {.column width="8%"}
:::

::: {.column .smaller width="55%"}
```{ojs}
// --- 1. REDRAW BUTTON & DATA GENERATOR ---

data = {
  redraw; // Reactive dependency: re-runs when button is clicked

  const labels = ['Guerre', 'Maladie', 'Finances', 'Relations', 'Moi', 'Persécution', 'Catastrophes', 'Cqrd', 'Spirituel'];

  const metadata = {
    'Guerre': { desc: 'Impact des conflits et guerres', url: 'https://example.com/guerre' },
    'Maladie': { desc: 'Sujets liés à la santé et aux maladies', url: 'https://example.com/maladie' },
    'Finances': { desc: 'Gestion financière et épreuves économiques', url: 'https://example.com/finances' },
    'Relations': { desc: 'Défis relationnels et sociaux', url: 'https://example.com/relations' },
    'Moi': { desc: 'Développement personnel et état d\'esprit', url: 'https://example.com/moi' },
    'Persécution': { desc: 'Expériences de discrimination ou de persécution', url: 'https://example.com/persecution' },
    'Catastrophes': { desc: 'Impact des événements naturels ou accidents', url: 'https://example.com/catastrophes' },
    'Cqrd': { desc: 'Catégorie CQRD', url: 'https://example.com/cqrd' },
    'Spirituel': { desc: 'Vie et action spirituelles', url: 'https://example.com/spirituel' }
  };

const minRatio = 0.10; // 5% minimum floor per item
  const count = labels.length;
  const remainingBudget = 1 - (minRatio); // Remaining weight to distribute (55% for 9 items)

  // 1. Generate random weights
  const rawData = labels.map(label => ({
    label,
    random: minRatio + remainingBudget*Math.random()
  }));

  const totalRandom = rawData.reduce((acc, d) => acc + d.random, 0);

  return {
    name: "root",
    children: [
      {
        name: "Categories",
        children: rawData.map(d => ({
          name: d.label,
          value: d.random ,
          desc: metadata[d.label].desc,
          url: metadata[d.label].url
        }))
      }
    ]
  };
}

// --- 2. CONFIGURATION ---
width = 800

height = 500

fontSize = "24px"

// --- 3. HIERARCHY CALCULATION ---
root = {
  const h = d3.hierarchy(data)
      .sum(d => d.value)
      .sort((a, b) => b.value - a.value);
  
  return d3.treemap()
      .size([width, height])
      .paddingInner(2)
      (h);
}

// --- 4. TOOLTIP ELEMENT ---
tooltip = d3.select("body").append("div")
    .style("position", "absolute")
    .style("visibility", "hidden")
    .style("background", "rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.85)")
    .style("color", "#fff")
    .style("padding", "8px 12px")
    .style("border-radius", "4px")
    .style("font-size", "12px")
    .style("pointer-events", "none")
    .style("z-index", "1000")
    .style("font-family", "sans-serif")

// --- 5. CHART RENDERING ---
chart = {
  const svg = d3.create("svg")
      .attr("viewBox", [0, 0, width, height])
      .attr("width", "100%")
      .attr("height", "auto")
      .style("font", "12px sans-serif");

  const leaf = svg.selectAll("g")
    .data(root.leaves())
    .join("g")
    .attr("transform", d => `translate(${d.x0},${d.y0})`);

  const link = leaf.append("a")
    .attr("xlink:href", d => d.data.url)
    .attr("target", "_blank")
    .style("cursor", "pointer");

  link.append("rect")
    .attr("fill", (d, i) => d3.schemeTableau10[i % 10])
    .attr("fill-opacity", 0.7)
    .attr("width", d => d.x1 - d.x0)
    .attr("height", d => d.y1 - d.y0)
    .attr("stroke", "white")
    .on("mouseover", function(event, d) {
      d3.select(this).attr("fill-opacity", 1);
      tooltip.style("visibility", "visible")
             .html(`<strong>${d.data.name}</strong><br/>${d.data.desc}<br/><em>Value: ${(d.value * 100).toFixed(1)}%</em>`);
    })
    .on("mousemove", function(event) {
      tooltip.style("top", (event.pageY - 10) + "px")
             .style("left", (event.pageX + 10) + "px");
    })
    .on("mouseout", function() {
      d3.select(this).attr("fill-opacity", 0.7);
      tooltip.style("visibility", "hidden");
    });

  link.append("text")
    .attr("x", d => (d.x1 - d.x0) / 2)
    .attr("y", d => (d.y1 - d.y0) / 2)
    .attr("dy", "0.35em")
    .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
    .attr("fill", "white")
    .attr("fill", "black") // <--- CHANGED FONT COLOR TO BLACK
    .style("font-size", fontSize)
    .style("font-weight", "bold")
    .style("pointer-events", "none")
    .text(d => (d.x1 - d.x0 > 50 && d.y1 - d.y0 > 25) ? d.data.name : "");

  return svg.node();
}
```

::: notes
#### 1. Introduction (Purpose: orient the listener)

- Present the **context** of the passage (historical, literary).

- State the dominant theme or **tension** the sermon will address.

- Give the sermon’s main idea (the **“Big Idea / Question”** or
  “Proposition”).

#### 2. Exposition of the Text (Verse-by-verse or section-by-section)

This is the backbone. Each movement explains what the text says and
means.

Usually structured as:

Point 1 — What the text says (explanation) **Explain** key words,
phrases, and ideas. Show how this part fits the passage’s flow.

Point 2 — Why it matters (theological significance) **Connect** the text
to biblical theology. Show what God is revealing about Himself,
humanity, or salvation.

Point 3 — How it applies (implication for life) Concrete, specific
**application**. Often includes examples, warnings, encouragements.

Each point follows the same mini‑pattern: **Explanation → Illustration →
Application**

#### 🧩 3. Illustrations (woven throughout)

Clarify difficult concepts.

Make abstract truths concrete.

Should illuminate the text, not distract from it.

#### 🎯 4. Application (specific, actionable, text‑rooted)

Application can be:

Personal (heart, habits, character)

Communal (church life)

Missional (witness, service)

Ethical (choices, behavior)

Good expository preaching ties each application directly to the text,
not to general moral advice.

#### 5. Conclusion

Restate the main idea.

Summarize the key movements of the text.

Call for a response (faith, obedience, trust, repentance).

End with prayer or reflection.
:::

![](ps44_toc.png)
:::
::::::

::: notes
🧱 Expository Sermon Skeleton — Psalm 44 Theme: When God feels absent,
faith remembers, laments, and pleads.

Big Idea: God’s past faithfulness becomes the foundation for honest
lament and bold prayer in present suffering.

I. Remembering God’s Past Faithfulness (vv. 1–8) Explanation:\
Israel recalls what God did for their ancestors—victories, deliverance,
covenant love. Their confidence was not in themselves but in God’s
power.

Illustration:\
A family photo album: remembering who you are by remembering where you
came from.

Application:

Faith begins with remembering.

Rehearse God’s past works in Scripture and in your own life.

Gratitude strengthens trust before hardship arrives.

II. Lamenting Present Confusion and Pain (vv. 9–16) Explanation:\
    The psalm shifts sharply: despite their faithfulness, they feel
    abandoned. They suffer defeat, humiliation, and shame. This is not
    rebellion—it is honest lament.

Illustration:\
A believer who keeps serving faithfully yet faces unexpected loss.

Application:

Scripture gives permission to say, “God, this doesn’t make sense.”

Lament is not unbelief; it is faith refusing to pretend.

Bring your confusion to God instead of burying it.

III. Affirming Covenant Loyalty Despite Suffering (vv. 17–22)
     Explanation:\
     Israel insists they have not turned away from God. Their suffering
     is not due to sin. Verse 22 becomes a key text later quoted by Paul
     (Rom 8:36).

Illustration:\
A soldier who remains loyal even when the battle seems unwinnable.

Application:

Obedience is not a guarantee of ease.

Faithfulness matters even when God feels silent.

Suffering can be part of God’s mysterious purposes.

IV. Pleading Boldly for God’s Intervention (vv. 23–26) Explanation:\
    The psalm ends with a cry: “Awake… Rise up… Redeem us.”\
    This is bold, urgent prayer grounded in God’s steadfast love.

Illustration:\
A child calling out in the night—not because they doubt the parent’s
love, but because they trust it.

Application:

Pray boldly when God feels distant.

Anchor your pleas in God’s character, not your performance.

Hope persists even when circumstances contradict it.

Conclusion Remember God’s past works.

Lament honestly before Him.

Remain faithful even in confusion.

Cry out boldly for His help. Psalm 44 teaches that mature faith is not
silent, stoic, or simplistic—it remembers, wrestles, and pleads.
:::
